source.title: Textual Steering Vectors Can Improve Visual Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models
source.authors: Woody Haosheng Gan; Deqing Fu; Julian Asilis; Ollie Liu; Dani Yogatama; Vatsal Sharan; Robin Jia; Willie Neiswanger

record.tranche_reason: The study extends SAE feature identification to visual concepts in text-only LLM backbones used by multimodal models, and reports that the identified concepts correspond to sparse sets of SAE features. It does not test superposition geometry or capacity competition.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is the reported count of SAE features associated with visual concepts in Figure 3. The visual steering accuracies and color-perception interventions in Sections 3–6 show effects of deliberately applied steering vectors; they do not test superposition, polysemanticity, or feature geometry.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained SAEs (GemmaScope, LlamaScope) to extract steering vectors and reports only steering performance on visual tasks. The Figure 3 counts come from its own selection pipeline: top-n activated features per anchor word, then filtered by o3-mini. That pipeline caps the number of features, so the small counts cannot show whether models hold sparse, SAE-recoverable features. No version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, but the emphasis needs correcting. The authors conclude that steering vectors derived from the text-only backbone (SAE, mean shift, probe) improve MLLM visual reasoning on CV-Bench and generalize out of distribution. Mean shift is the strongest method and prompting barely helps. The sparse SAE feature counts are a side remark, not a conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study extracts text-based SAE, mean-shift, and probe vectors and applies them to multimodal model activations; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: For the steering-performance experiments, results depend on the selected intervention method, token type, layer, and intervention strength; the reported SAE feature-count result does not establish sensitivity to these choices.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE feature directions taken from the text-only backbone (e.g. a GemmaScope 'red' feature) still causally shift the multimodal model's colour perception and task accuracy after vision-language post-training (Sec. 3, Table 1, Table 2). However, SAE vectors are generally weaker than mean-shift vectors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature directions learned on a text-only LLM remain causally meaningful in its multimodal fine-tuned descendant (cross-modal and post-training transfer of dictionary features).

record.problems: The feature-count evidence is limited to four selected visual-concept taxonomies and three text-only backbones. The text provides only the aggregate statement fewer than 10, not exact per-taxonomy or per-layer counts. The study does not test superposition geometry, feature overlap, or capacity pressure.
record.rows_left_out: Steering accuracy results in Tables 1–2 and the color-perception interventions in Figures 2 and 9 were left out because they measure deliberately induced steering effects, not the claim versions about superposition or SAE feature sparsity.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity transition, no feature geometry.
All: no capacity or dedicated-dimension analysis.
Whether LLM features spread across neurons, or whether SAEs recover sparse features: pretrained SAEs are only used as a tool.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' and its V4 'supports' label are rejected. The feature counts come from the study's own selection procedure, which is bounded by its top-n choice, and the paper does not treat them as evidence about superposition.

versions.untested_parts: Whether more sparse features than dimensions are represented by overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, and whether there is a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemantic neurons, or whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure, and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.

The study reports SAE feature counts for selected visual concepts in text-only backbones, but does not establish that LLM activations generally spread features across many neurons or that its results generalize beyond those concepts and models.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Whether features involved in superposition are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Counted SAE features associated with visual-concept taxonomies across layers.
rows.measure: Number of SAE features associated with each visual-concept taxonomy
rows.value: Fewer than 10 features per visual concept across 16k total SAE features.
rows.note: The paper gives this as an aggregate description; it does not state separate exact counts for each taxonomy or layer in the text.
rows.check: Selection value, not a test. The count is the output of the study's top-n plus o3-mini filter (Algorithm 1), so being 'fewer than 10' is bounded by n by construction. No baseline. It is unclear whether the count is before or after filtering. Exact per-layer values can only be read from a 3-D plot.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The four selected visual-concept taxonomies in the three tested text-only backbones
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports fewer than 10 associated SAE features per visual concept in each backbone’s much larger SAE dictionary, supporting the narrow claim that sparse SAE-recoverable features occur in these models (r1–r3).
